method_card.title: Cumulative Frequency and Box Plots
method_card.content:
Cumulative frequency is a running total of frequencies. To build a cumulative frequency table, add each frequency to the running total. The final cumulative frequency must equal the total number of values.

When plotting a cumulative frequency curve, plot each cumulative frequency against the upper boundary of its class (not the midpoint). Join the points with a smooth S-shaped curve (or straight lines for a cumulative frequency polygon). The curve always starts at (lower boundary of first class, 0).

For discrete data, a cumulative frequency step polygon is used: the frequency jumps at each exact value rather than being spread across an interval.

Reading off the curve to find quartiles: the median is at the \(\frac{n}{2}\)th value, Q1 is at the \(\frac{n}{4}\)th value, and Q3 is at the \(\frac{3n}{4}\)th value. Draw a horizontal line from the appropriate cumulative frequency, read across to the curve, then drop down to the x-axis.

The interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1. It measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is less affected by extreme values than the full range.

A box plot (box-and-whisker diagram) shows five values: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box spans Q1 to Q3; the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum (or to fences if outliers are excluded at Higher tier). When comparing two box plots, always state a numerical comparison of medians and a numerical comparison of spreads (range or IQR), then interpret both in context.
steps: Build the cumulative frequency column by running total
Plot each cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary
Join with a smooth curve (or step polygon for discrete data)
Read the median at n/2, Q1 at n/4, Q3 at 3n/4 from the curve
For box plot comparison: state median comparison AND spread comparison, both in context

exam_context.marks: 3–6 marks; reading median/Q1/Q3 from a given curve is 3 marks; comparing two box plots in context is 3–4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Cumulative frequency curves and box plot comparison appear on almost every paper; the IQR calculation and context comparison are the most-tested Higher extensions

worked_examples.question: A cumulative frequency curve shows data for 40 values. At what cumulative frequency should you read to find the median?

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Draw a horizontal line from cumulative frequency = 20 to the curve, then drop down to find the median.

worked_examples.question: A cumulative frequency table for the masses (kg) of 60 parcels shows: ≤5 kg: 8; ≤10 kg: 23; ≤15 kg: 44; ≤20 kg: 55; ≤25 kg: 60. Estimate the median mass from the table.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the median position
steps.content: Median is at the \(\frac{60}{2} = 30\)th value. The cumulative frequency passes 30 in the class ≤15 kg (cf = 44 ≥ 30, while cf at ≤10 kg = 23 < 30).

steps.label: Step 2 — Interpolate within the class 10–15
steps.content: Need the 30th value. 23 values are ≤10 kg, so the 7th value in the 10–15 class. Class has \(44 - 23 = 21\) values. Estimate: \(10 + \frac{7}{21} \times 5 \approx 10 + 1.67 \approx 11.7\) kg.

worked_examples.question: Two box plots show the waiting times (minutes) at two call centres. Centre A: min 2, Q1 8, median 14, Q3 22, max 35. Centre B: min 1, Q1 5, median 10, Q3 16, max 28. Compare the two distributions fully in context.

steps.label: Step 1 — Compare medians
steps.content: Centre A median = 14 min; Centre B median = 10 min. Centre B has shorter typical waiting times by 4 minutes.

steps.label: Step 2 — Compare spread (IQR)
steps.content: Centre A IQR = 22 − 8 = 14 min. Centre B IQR = 16 − 5 = 11 min. Centre B's waiting times are more consistent (smaller IQR).

steps.label: Step 3 — Interpret in context
steps.content: Centre B provides shorter waits on average and more predictable service. Centre A not only makes customers wait longer but also has more variable waiting times, making it harder for callers to plan.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Centre B has a lower median (10 vs 14 min) and a smaller IQR (11 vs 14 min), meaning it is both faster and more consistent for callers. Centre A has longer and less predictable waits.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency table shows 80 values. At what cumulative frequency do you read to find Q1?

misconceptions.message: Q1 is at the n/4 position: 80/4 = 20. Don't use n/4 + 1 or 3n/4.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency table shows: ≤10: 5; ≤20: 18; ≤30: 34; ≤40: 45; ≤50: 50. What is the cumulative frequency at ≤30?

misconceptions.message: Read the cumulative frequency directly from the table: at ≤30 it is 34. This is a running total, not the class frequency.

bronze.display: A box plot shows Q1 = 15 and Q3 = 35. What is the IQR?

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 35 − 15 = 20. Do not confuse IQR with the full range.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency curve reaches a maximum of 60. At what cumulative frequency position is Q3?

misconceptions.message: Q3 is at 3n/4 = 3×60/4 = 45. Don't use n/4 or n/2 for Q3.

bronze.display: A box plot for exam scores shows: minimum 30, Q1 48, median 62, Q3 74, maximum 90. What is the range?

misconceptions.message: Range = maximum − minimum = 90 − 30 = 60. Don't use Q3 − Q1 for the range.

bronze.display: A cumulative frequency table for heights (cm) shows: ≤150: 4; ≤160: 19; ≤170: 35; ≤180: 46; ≤190: 50. What is the class frequency for the 160–170 interval?

misconceptions.message: Class frequency = difference between consecutive cumulative frequencies: 35 − 19 = 16.

bronze.display: A box plot has median 25 and IQR 18. What are Q1 and Q3?

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 18. The box is symmetric around the median: Q1 = 25 − 9 = 16, Q3 = 25 + 9 = 34. Note: the box need not be symmetric in general — this problem states IQR=18 with the median at the midpoint of the box.

bronze.display: When plotting a cumulative frequency curve for grouped continuous data, the points are plotted against which value in each class?
options: The midpoint of the class
The lower class boundary
The upper class boundary
The class frequency

misconceptions.message: Plot cumulative frequency against the upper class boundary. Plotting against the midpoint is correct for a frequency polygon, not a CF curve.

silver.display: A cumulative frequency table for 40 values shows: ≤20: 6; ≤30: 18; ≤40: 30; ≤50: 37; ≤60: 40. Estimate the median by interpolation within the appropriate class.

misconceptions.message: Median at 20th value. 18 values ≤30, 30 values ≤40, so median is in class 30–40. Need 2nd value in this class (12 values). Interpolation: 30 + (2/12)×10 = 30 + 1.67 ≈ 31.7. Check reading: n=40, median position = 20. cf at 30 is 18, cf at 40 is 30. Need 2nd of the 12 in class 30–40. Value = 30 + (2/12)×10 ≈ 31.7.

silver.display: A box plot for Group X shows: min 10, Q1 20, median 30, Q3 42, max 60. A box plot for Group Y shows: min 5, Q1 22, median 35, Q3 48, max 65. Which group has the larger IQR?
options: Group X (IQR = 22)
Group Y (IQR = 26)
Both groups have the same IQR
Cannot tell from the box plots

misconceptions.message: IQR X = 42 − 20 = 22. IQR Y = 48 − 22 = 26. Group Y has the larger IQR, meaning more spread in the middle 50%.

silver.display: A cumulative frequency table for 60 students' scores shows the median estimated at 54 and Q3 estimated at 68. What is the value at which Q1 should be read from the curve?

misconceptions.message: Q1 is at cumulative frequency n/4 = 60/4 = 15. Draw a horizontal line from cf = 15 to the curve.

silver.display: Two box plots compare delivery times for two couriers. Courier A: median 3 days, IQR 2 days. Courier B: median 4 days, IQR 1 day. A manager wants the most consistent courier. Which should they choose and why?
options: Courier A — lower median means faster on average, which is more consistent
Courier B — smaller IQR means more consistent delivery times despite the higher median
Courier A — lower IQR means more consistent delivery times
Courier B — higher median means more reliable

misconceptions.message: Consistency is measured by spread (IQR). Courier B's IQR = 1 day (smaller) means its times cluster more tightly around the median. Courier A is faster on average but less predictable.

silver.display: A cumulative frequency table shows: ≤5: 3; ≤10: 11; ≤15: 23; ≤20: 31; ≤25: 35. What is the total number of values in the dataset?

misconceptions.message: The total frequency equals the final cumulative frequency: 35. Do not add the cumulative frequencies together.

silver.display: A box plot shows Q1 = 12, median = 20, Q3 = 31 for 44 students' test scores. Find the IQR.

misconceptions.message: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 31 − 12 = 19. Do not include the median in this calculation.

gold.display: Two cumulative frequency curves represent the heights of 80 students in each of two schools. School A: median 162 cm, Q1 155 cm, Q3 170 cm. School B: median 165 cm, Q1 160 cm, Q3 172 cm. Write a full comparison of the two distributions in context.
options: School B students are taller on average (median 165 vs 162 cm) and slightly more consistent (IQR 12 vs 15 cm for A). On average, School B students are 3 cm taller.
School A students are taller on average and more varied in height.
Both schools have similar median heights; School B has a larger IQR.
School B is taller on average but School A is more consistent (larger IQR means more spread).

misconceptions.message: IQR A = 170 − 155 = 15 cm. IQR B = 172 − 160 = 12 cm. B has higher median (taller) and smaller IQR (more consistent). Both comparisons must include the context (heights, schools) and numerical values.

gold.display: A cumulative frequency table for 100 values shows: ≤10: 8; ≤20: 25; ≤30: 58; ≤40: 82; ≤50: 100. Find Q1 and Q3 by interpolation.

misconceptions.message: Q1 at cf=25: exactly at ≤20 boundary. Q1 = 20. Q3 at cf=75: in class 30–40 (cf goes from 58 to 82). Need 17th of 24 values: 30 + (17/24)×10 = 30 + 7.08 ≈ 37.1.

gold.display: A cumulative frequency curve for exam scores (out of 80) for 120 students gives Q1 = 38, median = 52, Q3 = 64. The pass mark is 45. Estimate the number of students who passed.

misconceptions.message: Read off the CF curve at score 45 to get the number who scored ≤45. Estimate: 45 lies between Q1=38 (cf=30) and median=52 (cf=60). Interpolate: cf ≈ 30 + ((45−38)/(52−38)) × 30 = 30 + (7/14)×30 = 30+15 = 45. Passed = 120 − 45 = 75.

gold.display: Two box plots compare salaries (£000s) at two companies. Company X: min 18, Q1 24, median 32, Q3 44, max 80. Company Y: min 20, Q1 28, median 36, Q3 46, max 62. A job-seeker values consistency over average salary. Which company offers more consistent salaries?
options: Company X — lower minimum salary means less variation at the bottom
Company X — larger range means the data is more spread, which some define as consistent
Company Y — smaller IQR (18 vs 20) and smaller range (42 vs 62) both point to greater consistency
Company Y — higher median automatically means more consistent pay

misconceptions.message: IQR X = 44−24 = 20; IQR Y = 46−28 = 18. Range X = 80−18 = 62; Range Y = 62−20 = 42. Company Y has smaller IQR and smaller range: both measures of spread are lower, confirming greater consistency.

gold.display: A cumulative frequency table for discrete data (number of absences per student, 0–10) has 63 values. The table gives: 0: 5; 1: 12; 2: 14; 3: 11; 4: 8; 5: 6; 6: 4; 7: 2; 8: 1. A step polygon is drawn. At what y-value does the step rise when x changes from 2 to 3?

misconceptions.message: For a step polygon, the step at x=3 rises to the cumulative frequency up to and including 3 absences: 5+12+14+11 = 42. But the step rises from cf at x=2 (5+12+14=31) to cf at x=3 (42). The y-value after the step at x=3 is 42; the y-value before the step (i.e. at x=2) is 31.
